B01-Q011.question: A life insurance policy was issued on January 15, 2024. The insured made a material misrepresentation on the application regarding a pre-existing heart condition. The insurer discovers the false statement on March 1, 2026. Can the insurer void the policy?
options: Yes, because a false statement on an application always voids the policy
Yes, because the insurer discovered the false statement during the term of the policy
No, because the 2-year incontestability period has passed and the insurer can no longer challenge the policy for misstatement.
No, because a material misrepresentation must be discovered within 12 months of issuance
B01-Q011.correctAnswer: No, because the 2-year incontestability period has passed and the insurer can no longer challenge the policy for misstatement.
B01-Q011.explanation: The incontestability clause states that after a life insurance policy has been in effect for two years during the life of the insured, the insurer cannot contest the policy based on a material misrepresentation in the application. The policy was issued on January 15, 2024. As of March 1, 2026, more than two years have passed, so the policy is incontestable.

optionExplanations.Yes, because a false statement on an app: A false statement does not always void a policy. After the incontestability period expires, the insurer loses the right to challenge coverage based on incorrect statements on the application.
optionExplanations.Yes, because the insurer discovered the: The timing of discovery alone is not the determining factor. The important thing is whether the incontestable period has expired. Once two years have passed with the policy in force during the life of the insured, the insurer's right to challenge is extinguished.
optionExplanations.No, because a material misrepresentation: There is no 12-month discovery rule for false statements. The standard incontestable period in life insurance is two years, not one.

B01-Q006.question: The annual premium for a life insurance policy was due on February 1, but has not been paid. Under the standard grace period provision, until what date will the policy remain in force?
options: February 10
February 28
March 3
March 4
B01-Q006.explanation: Life insurance policies provide a 31-day grace period after the premium due date. With a due date of February 1, the policyholder has until March 4 (31 days later) to pay the premium due while the policy remains in force.

optionExplanations.February 10: February 10th is just 9 days after the due date. This confuses the grace period with the free-look period.
optionExplanations.February 28: February 28 is only 27 days, which does not meet the 31-day grace period requirement.
optionExplanations.March 3: March 3 is 30 days after the due date. The grace period in life insurance is 31 days, not 30.

B01-Q009.question: An employee covered under an employer-sponsored group term life insurance plan terminates employment. Under the group conversion privilege, which of the following statements is TRUE?
options: The employee can convert to an individual term policy for the same face amount without evidence of insurability within 31 days
Employee may convert to an individual whole life policy for an equal or lower face amount without evidence of insurability within 31 days
Employee must submit a new application with full medical underwriting within 60 days after termination
Employee loses all coverage immediately upon termination of employment with no conversion option
B01-Q009.correctAnswer: Employee may convert to an individual whole life policy for an equal or lower face amount without evidence of insurability within 31 days
B01-Q009.explanation: The group conversion privilege allows an employee terminating employment to convert group coverage to an individual whole life (non-term) policy for the same or lower face amount, without evidence of insurability, provided the conversion is requested within 31 days after termination.

optionExplanations.The employee can convert to an individua: Conversion under group policies is to an individual whole life (permanent) policy, not a term policy. This is a key distinction that is tested on the exam.
optionExplanations.Employee must submit a new application w: The conversion privilege exists precisely so that the employee does not have to provide evidence of insurability. No medical underwriting is required, and the term is 31 days, not 60.
optionExplanations.Employee loses all coverage immediately: Group policies include a conversion privilege as a standard provision. Coverage does not simply disappear upon termination of employment. The employee has 31 days to exercise the conversion right.

B01-Q010.question: A 67-year-old client enrolled in Original Medicare is comparing a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) policy with a Medicare Advantage plan. Which statement about Medicare Supplement policies is TRUE?
options: Medicare Supplement plans use provider networks and require referrals to specialists
Medicare Supplement plans are standardized, meaning each plan letter (A through N) offers the same benefits no matter which insurer issues the policy
Medicare Supplement plans replace Original Medicare and provide all benefits directly
Medicare Supplement premiums are set by CMS and are identical among all insurance companies
B01-Q010.correctAnswer: Medicare Supplement plans are standardized, meaning each plan letter (A through N) offers the same benefits no matter which insurer issues the policy
B01-Q010.explanation: Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plans are standardized at the federal level. Each plan letter (A, B, C, D, F, G, K, L, M, N) provides the same basic benefits no matter which insurer issues it. The insured can see any provider who accepts Medicare. Only the premiums vary depending on the insurer.

optionExplanations.Medicare Supplement plans use provider n: Medicare Supplement policies do not use provider networks or require referrals. That describes Medicare Advantage (Part C) plans, which can use HMO or PPO network structures.
optionExplanations.Medicare Supplement plans replace Origin: Medicare Supplement policies do not replace Original Medicare. They supplement it by covering some of the out-of-pocket costs (deductibles, copayments, coinsurance) that Original Medicare does not pay.
optionExplanations.Medicare Supplement premiums are set by: Although the benefits of each plan letter are standardized, premiums are set individually by each insurer and can vary significantly. CMS does not set Medigap premiums.

B01-Q004.question: A 28-year-old client with a young family and a tight budget wants coverage that will protect her dependents for the next 20 years while her children are growing up. What type of policy BEST fits this need?
B01-Q004.subdomain: Term Insurance vs. whole life insurance
options: 20-year level term life insurance
Whole life insurance
Single Premium Whole Life Insurance
Variable universal life insurance
B01-Q004.explanation: A 20-year level term policy provides a death benefit during the specified period of need at the lowest premium cost. It fits exactly the client's temporary need for protection and her budget limitation.

optionExplanations.Whole life insurance: Whole life insurance provides permanent coverage and builds cash value, but its premium is significantly higher. Given the tight budget and a defined 20-year need, term insurance is the best option.
optionExplanations.Single Premium Whole Life Insurance: Single premium whole life insurance requires a large lump sum payment, which contradicts the tight budget requirement. It is designed for wealth transfer, not affordable temporary protection.
optionExplanations.Variable universal life insurance: Variable universal life insurance carries investment risk, has higher costs, and is more complex. It does not align with a simple need for temporary protection on a limited budget.

B01-Q007.question: A potential buyer inquires about a policy that allows flexible premium payments and credits interest at a rate stated by the insurer, but never below a guaranteed minimum. What product is the agent describing?
options: variable life insurance
Variable universal life insurance
Universal life insurance
Indexed universal life insurance
B01-Q007.explanation: Universal life features flexible premiums and a cash value that earns interest at a current rate stated by the insurer, with a guaranteed minimum floor. The insurer, not the policyholder, assumes the investment risk in the general account.

optionExplanations.variable life insurance: Variable life has fixed scheduled premiums and invests the cash value in separate accounts chosen by the policyholder. The investment risk rests with the policyholder and there is no guaranteed minimum interest rate.
optionExplanations.Variable universal life insurance: Variable universal life combines flexible premiums with investment options in separate accounts. Because the policyholder directs the investments, the cash value can fluctuate below a guaranteed floor, unlike the scenario described.
optionExplanations.Indexed universal life insurance: Indexed universal life credits interest based on the performance of an external index (such as the S&P 500), not a rate declared by the insurer. Although it may have a floor, the crediting mechanism differs from a declared current rate.

B01-Q001.question: An agent delivers a new life insurance policy to the insured on March 1. The insured reads the policy and decides that the coverage does not meet her needs. Under Texas law, what is the last day the policyholder can return the policy for a full refund of premium?
options: March 10
March 11
March 31
April 1
B01-Q001.explanation: Texas establishes a 10-day free look period that begins on the date the policy is delivered. If delivery was on March 1, the insured has until March 11 (10 full days after delivery) to return the policy for a full refund of premium.

optionExplanations.March 10: March 10th is just 9 days after delivery. The free-look period is 10 days, not 9.
optionExplanations.March 31: March 31 represents a 30-day period, which confuses the free-look period with the premium payment grace period.
optionExplanations.April 1: April 1 represents 31 days, which corresponds to the grace period for premium payment on life insurance, not the free-look period.

B01-Q003.question: Maria is enrolled in a Texas HMO plan. She has recurring knee pain and wants to see an orthopedic specialist. What should Maria do FIRST under a standard HMO plan?
options: Schedule an appointment directly with any in-network orthopedic specialist
Get a referral from your primary care doctor
Submit a prior authorization request to the HMO claims department
Visit an out-of-network specialist and file a claim for reimbursement
B01-Q003.correctAnswer: Get a referral from your primary care doctor
B01-Q003.explanation: HMO plans operate under a gatekeeper model. The enrolled member must first consult her assigned primary care physician, who evaluates the condition and provides a referral to a specialist within the HMO network if medically necessary.

optionExplanations.Schedule an appointment directly with an: This describes how a PPO works, not an HMO. In an HMO, members cannot see specialists on their own without first getting a referral from the PCP.
optionExplanations.Submit a prior authorization request to: Prior authorization may be required for certain procedures, but the access control step (PCP referral) comes first in an HMO before any specialist visit or authorization request.
optionExplanations.Visit an out-of-network specialist and f: HMO plans generally do not cover out-of-network services except in emergencies. Visiting an out-of-network specialist without authorization would likely result in the member assuming the entire cost.

B01-Q012.question: An HMO member is on vacation out of state when she experiences severe chest pain and is admitted to the nearest emergency room, which is not in her HMO's network. How will the HMO handle this claim?
options: The HMO will deny the claim because all services must be obtained from network providers
The HMO must cover emergency services because emergency care is covered regardless of network status
The HMO will cover only 50% of the emergency room bill as a penalty for being out of network
Member must transfer to an in-network hospital within 24 hours or claim will be denied
B01-Q012.correctAnswer: The HMO must cover emergency services because emergency care is covered regardless of network status
B01-Q012.explanation: HMO plans are required to cover emergency medical services regardless of whether the provider is in-network or out-of-network. A true medical emergency (such as severe chest pain) activates coverage at the emergency center without prior authorization or network restriction.

optionExplanations.The HMO will deny the claim because all: Although HMOs generally restrict coverage to in-network providers, emergency services are the exception. Denying a genuine emergency claim based solely on network status would violate regulatory requirements.
optionExplanations.The HMO will cover only 50% of the emerg: Emergency services in a true emergency are not subject to out-of-network penalties in the same way as elective services. The plan must cover the emergency at the normal level of benefits.
optionExplanations.Member must transfer to an in-network ho: There is no general requirement to transfer within 24 hours. Once stabilized, follow-up care may need to return to the network, but initial emergency treatment is covered regardless.

B01-Q013.question: A business partner applies for a life insurance policy on the life of her co-owner, naming herself as beneficiary. The co-owner consents to the request. Is there insurable interest?
options: No, because insurable interest only exists between spouses and blood relatives.
No, because the beneficiary and the insured are not the same person
Yes, because a business partner has an insurable interest in the life of a co-owner whose death would cause financial loss to the business.
Yes, but only if the face amount of the policy does not exceed the value of the business
B01-Q013.correctAnswer: Yes, because a business partner has an insurable interest in the life of a co-owner whose death would cause financial loss to the business.
B01-Q013.explanation: Insurable interest exists when the applicant would suffer financial loss upon the death of the insured. A business partner has an insurable interest in a co-owner because the death of the co-owner could financially harm the business. Insurable interest is required at the time of application, and consent was granted.

optionExplanations.No, because insurable interest only exis: Insurable interest extends beyond family relationships. Business associates, key employees, creditors and others with a financial interest in the continued life of the insured qualify.
optionExplanations.No, because the beneficiary and the insu: The beneficiary and the insured do not have to be the same person. Third party ownership is common in business insurance arrangements as long as there is an insurable interest at the time of application.
optionExplanations.Yes, but only if the face amount of the: Although the face amount must bear a reasonable relationship to the financial interest, there is no rigid legal requirement that the death benefit exactly match the value of the business. The key requirement is that there is insurable interest at the outset.

B01-Q014.question: A whole life policyholder stops paying premiums after 15 years and does not choose a non-lapse option. Under the standard no-forfeiture provision, which option will the insurer automatically apply?
options: Term insurance extended for the face amount of the policy
Reduced Whole Life Insurance Paid
Cash surrender of the entire policy
Automatic Cash Value Premium Loan
B01-Q014.correctAnswer: Term insurance extended for the face amount of the policy
B01-Q014.explanation: When a whole life policyholder stops paying premiums and does not actively elect a non-lapse option, the automatic (default) non-lapse option is extended term insurance. The insurer uses the existing cash value to purchase term insurance for the original face amount, which lasts as long as the cash value can support it.

optionExplanations.Reduced Whole Life Insurance Paid: Paid Reduced Insurance is an available non-forfeiture option, but is not the automatic default option. The policyholder must affirmatively choose it.
optionExplanations.Cash surrender of the entire policy: The cash surrender terminates the policy and pays the cash value. This is an elective option, not the default automatic option when no choice is made.
optionExplanations.Automatic Cash Value Premium Loan: An automatic premium loan is a separate policy provision that uses the cash value to pay the premium due. This is different from the default non-forfeiture option and must be chosen or included in the policy as a rider.

B01-Q018.question: A member of a PPO plan needs to see a dermatologist. Under a typical PPO arrangement, what must the member do?
options: Get a referral from a primary care doctor before visiting the specialist
Choose any dermatologist, but the member will pay less if the provider is in-network
Visit only dermatologists within the PPO network; out-of-network visits are never covered
Submit a prior authorization form to the insurer at least 14 days before the appointment
B01-Q018.correctAnswer: Choose any dermatologist, but the member will pay less if the provider is in-network
B01-Q018.explanation: PPO plans allow members to see any provider without a referral. Members receive the highest level of benefits when using in-network providers, but out-of-network providers are also covered at a reduced benefit level. No access control or reference required.

optionExplanations.Get a referral from a primary care docto: This describes how an HMO works. PPOs do not require a PCP referral to see a specialist.
optionExplanations.Visit only dermatologists within the PPO: PPO plans do cover out-of-network visits, although at a higher cost to the member. Unlike HMOs, PPOs do not restrict coverage exclusively to in-network providers.
optionExplanations.Submit a prior authorization form to the: Although some procedures may require prior authorization under any type of plan, there is no standard 14-day prior authorization requirement for routine visits to specialists under a PPO.

B01-Q016.question: Under Texas law, which of the following is a required provision in a long-term care insurance policy?
options: A 90-day elimination period with no exceptions
Coverage for skilled nursing care only
A non-lapse benefit option or a contingent benefit upon policy lapse
Unlimited duration of lifetime benefits
B01-Q016.correctAnswer: A non-lapse benefit option or a contingent benefit upon policy lapse
B01-Q016.explanation: Texas regulations require long-term care policies to offer a non-lapse benefit option or a contingent benefit upon policy expiration. This consumer protection ensures that the policyholder retains some value even if the policy lapses after significant premium payments.

optionExplanations.A 90-day elimination period with no exce: LTC policies may offer various elimination period options (30, 60, 90 days, etc.), but a 90-day period is not universally required. The elimination period is typically selected by the policyholder.
optionExplanations.Coverage for skilled nursing care only: LTC policies cover a variety of levels of care, including custodial care, assisted living, home health care, and adult day care, not just skilled nursing.
optionExplanations.Unlimited duration of lifetime benefits: Unlimited benefit duration is an optional feature, not a regulatory requirement. Many LTC policies have a maximum benefit period (for example, 3 or 5 years).

B01-Q020.question: Which of the following BEST describes the primary purpose of an annuity?
options: Provide a death benefit to named beneficiaries
Provide a systematic settlement of a sum of money over a period of time, typically as retirement income
Protect the insured against the financial consequences of a disability
Create tax-free savings for a child's educational expenses
B01-Q020.correctAnswer: Provide a systematic settlement of a sum of money over a period of time, typically as retirement income
B01-Q020.explanation: The primary purpose of an annuity is to provide periodic income payments, typically during retirement. An annuity systematically liquidates an accumulated sum over time, protecting the annuitant against the risk of outliving his or her savings (longevity risk).

optionExplanations.Provide a death benefit to named benefic: Providing a death benefit is the primary purpose of life insurance, not annuities. Although some annuities include death benefit features, the central purpose is income distribution.
optionExplanations.Protect the insured against the financia: Protection against loss of disability income is the purpose of disability income insurance, not an annuity.
optionExplanations.Create tax-free savings for a child's ed: Education savings are typically managed through 529 plans or Coverdell accounts. Annuities are not designed as educational savings vehicles and carry tax penalties for early withdrawal.

B01-Q019.question: When a person enrolls in a health insurance plan, HIPAA requires that the insurer:
options: Share the enrollee's medical information with the enrollee's employer upon request
Provide the enrollee with a Notice of Privacy Practices that explains how protected health information may be used and disclosed
Destroy all medical records within 30 days of the enrollment decision
Obtain written consent from the enrollee before disclosing medical information to any government agency, including regulators
B01-Q019.correctAnswer: Provide the enrollee with a Notice of Privacy Practices that explains how protected health information may be used and disclosed
B01-Q019.explanation: Under 45 CFR §164.520, health plans must provide a Notice of Privacy Practices to new enrollees at the time of enrollment. The notice explains how the plan may use and disclose protected health information (PHI), describes the individual's privacy rights, and identifies how complaints can be made. The plan must also send a reminder at least once every three years that the notice is available upon request.

optionExplanations.Share the enrollee's medical information: HIPAA restricts the disclosure of PHI. Sharing an enrollee's health information with an employer without proper authorization would be a violation of HIPAA, not a requirement.
optionExplanations.Destroy all medical records within 30 da: HIPAA does not require destruction of records within 30 days. Privacy policies, procedures, and related documentation must be retained for at least six years under HIPAA records retention requirements.
optionExplanations.Obtain written consent from the enrollee: HIPAA allows certain disclosures to government agencies for public health, law enforcement, and regulatory oversight without individual consent. Written consent of the enrollee is not required in all government disclosure scenarios.

B01-Q021.question: A 65-year-old person enrolls in Medicare Part B and applies for a Medigap policy during their 6-month open enrollment period. You had continuous employer group health coverage for the previous 10 years. Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding your Medigap enrollment?
options: The insurer may deny your application based on your health history during the open enrollment period
The insurer must accept her request and cannot impose a pre-existing condition waiting period because she has more than 6 months of prior creditable coverage
The insurer must accept your request, but may impose up to a 12-month waiting period for a pre-existing condition regardless of prior coverage.
The insurer may charge you a higher premium based on pre-existing health conditions during open enrollment
B01-Q021.correctAnswer: The insurer must accept her request and cannot impose a pre-existing condition waiting period because she has more than 6 months of prior creditable coverage
B01-Q021.explanation: During Medigap's 6-month open enrollment period (which begins the month a person is age 65 or older and enrolled in Part B), insurers cannot deny coverage or charge higher premiums based on health status. Federal law allows insurers to impose up to a 6-month waiting period for pre-existing conditions, but this period must be reduced month by month for any prior creditable coverage. Because this applicant had 10 continuous years of employer group coverage, her creditable coverage exceeds 6 months, so the insurer cannot impose any waiting period.

optionExplanations.The insurer may deny your application ba: During the Medigap open enrollment period, insurers cannot deny an applicant based on their health history. Guaranteed issue applies: Any Medigap plan sold in the state must be offered regardless of medical condition.
optionExplanations.The insurer must accept your request, bu: The maximum waiting period for a pre-existing condition under federal law is 6 months, not 12 months. Additionally, the waiting period is reduced by prior creditable coverage. With 10 years of continuous employer coverage, this applicant would not face any waiting period.
optionExplanations.The insurer may charge you a higher prem: During the open enrollment period, insurers cannot use health status to increase premiums. The applicant is entitled to the same rate offered to other enrollees of the same age and profile, without a surcharge based on health.

B01-Q022.question: A policyholder names his wife as the primary beneficiary and his two adult children as contingent beneficiaries in equal shares. The wife dies before the insured. The insured dies without changing the beneficiary designation. Who receives the death benefit?
options: The succession of the insured
The two children, each receiving 50% as contingent beneficiaries
The wife's estate, because she was the named primary beneficiary
The insurer holds the funds until a court determines the legitimate recipient.
B01-Q022.correctAnswer: The two children, each receiving 50% as contingent beneficiaries
B01-Q022.explanation: When the primary beneficiary dies before the insured, the death benefit passes to the contingent (secondary) beneficiaries. The two adult children, named as equal contingent beneficiaries, each receive 50% of the death benefit.

optionExplanations.The succession of the insured: The death benefit goes to the estate only if there are no surviving beneficiaries (primary or contingent). Here, both contingent beneficiaries are alive.
optionExplanations.The wife's estate, because she was the n: The estate of a deceased primary beneficiary does not automatically inherit the death benefit. The funds pass to the contingent beneficiaries, not to the deceased primary beneficiary's estate.
optionExplanations.The insurer holds the funds until a cour: The insurer does not retain the funds. The policy's beneficiary designation governs distribution. Contingent beneficiaries receive funds when the primary beneficiary has died.

B03-Q003.question: The owner of a participating whole life insurance policy receives an annual dividend from the policy. Which of the following is a standard dividend option?
options: Use the dividend to purchase one-year term insurance (paid additions option)
Apply the dividend to increase the policy's guaranteed interest rate
Using the dividend to reduce the policy's death benefit
Use the dividend to purchase additional fully paid whole life insurance
B03-Q003.correctAnswer: Use the dividend to purchase additional fully paid whole life insurance
B03-Q003.explanation: A standard dividend option allows the policyholder to use the dividends to purchase additional small amounts of fully paid whole life insurance. This increases the total death benefit and cash value without additional underwriting. Other standard options include receiving dividends in cash, applying them to reduce premiums, leaving them on deposit with interest, or purchasing one-year term insurance add-ons.

optionExplanations.Use the dividend to purchase one-year te: Using dividends to purchase one-year term insurance is known as the fifth dividend option or the one-year term insurance option, not the paid-up additions option. The description in this answer incorrectly labels the option name. The paid additions option purchases permanent whole life coverage, not one-year term insurance.
optionExplanations.Apply the dividend to increase the polic: Dividends cannot be used to change the guaranteed interest rate stated in the policy. The guaranteed rate is a contractual provision set when the policy is issued and cannot be adjusted by dividend election.
optionExplanations.Using the dividend to reduce the policy': Dividends are designed to benefit the policyholder, not reduce the death benefit. Neither standard dividend option results in a lower death benefit.

B01-Q024.question: A life insurance beneficiary wants to receive the death benefit in equal monthly payments for a fixed number of years. Which settlement option should the beneficiary select?
options: Lifetime income option
Fixed period option (installment payments for a fixed period)
Interest only option
Lump Sum Option
B01-Q024.correctAnswer: Fixed period option (installment payments for a fixed period)
B01-Q024.explanation: The fixed period settlement option (installment payments for a fixed period) pays equal installments over a chosen number of years until funds and interest are exhausted. This coincides with the beneficiary's request to receive equal monthly payments for a defined time.

optionExplanations.Lifetime income option: The lifetime income option pays installments over the entire life of the beneficiary, not over a set number of years. The length of payments depends on how long the beneficiary lives, not a fixed period.
optionExplanations.Interest only option: The interest-only option leaves the principal with the insurer and pays only the interest earned. The principal is not distributed in installments under this option.
optionExplanations.Lump Sum Option: The lump sum option pays the entire death benefit at once, not as monthly installments over a period of years.

B03-Q001.question: A life insurance policy was issued on June 1, 2024. The insured dies by suicide on March 15, 2025. The policy contains a standard 2-year suicide exclusion. What will the insurance company pay?
options: The total nominal amount, because suicide is always covered under life insurance
Nothing, because suicide voids the policy completely and no benefits are ever paid
Refund of premiums paid, because the death occurred within the suicide exclusion period
Half of the face amount as a compromise agreement
B03-Q001.correctAnswer: Refund of premiums paid, because the death occurred within the suicide exclusion period
B03-Q001.explanation: The standard suicide clause states that if the insured dies by suicide within two years from the date of issue of the policy, the insurer's liability is limited to returning the premiums paid. The policy was issued on June 1, 2024, and the death occurred on March 15, 2025, which is within the 2-year exclusion period. After the exclusion period expires, suicide is covered like any other cause of death.

optionExplanations.The total nominal amount, because suicid: Suicide is not always covered. During the exclusion period (usually the first two years), the insurer's obligation is limited to returning the premiums paid. Suicide coverage applies only after the exclusion period has passed.
optionExplanations.Nothing, because suicide voids the polic: The suicide clause does not void the policy entirely or deny all payment. Limits the insurer's liability to return premiums paid during the exclusion period. The beneficiary still receives the premium refund.
optionExplanations.Half of the face amount as a compromise: There is no compromise provision for half a benefit in the suicide clause. The insurer returns the premiums paid, not a fraction of the face amount.

B03-Q006.question: A Texas HMO conducts utilization review to evaluate the medical necessity of proposed treatments. Under Texas law, who must make the final determination that a requested service is not medically necessary?
options: A claims examiner without medical training
A licensed doctor
The affiliate's employer
The commissioner of the Texas Department of Insurance personally
B03-Q006.explanation: Texas law requires that adverse determinations related to medical necessity in utilization review be made by, or under the supervision of, a licensed physician. A non-physician claims processor may handle an initial administrative review, but the final decision to deny a service for medical necessity must involve physician-level review.

optionExplanations.A claims examiner without medical traini: A claims examiner without medical training can perform an initial administrative review, but cannot make the final determination of medical necessity. That decision requires clinical judgment at a medical level under Texas law.
optionExplanations.The affiliate's employer: The enrollee's employer has no role in utilization review or medical necessity determinations. Those decisions are made within the HMO's clinical review process.
optionExplanations.The commissioner of the Texas Department: The TDI commissioner oversees regulatory compliance, but does not personally make individual medical necessity determinations for HMO enrollees. That is the role of HMO medical reviewers.

B03-Q002.question: The owner of a whole life policy stopped paying premiums and the policy expired 8 months ago. The policyholder now wants to reinstate the policy. Under the standard rehabilitation provision, which of the following requirements is the insurer MOST LIKELY to require?
options: A new application with full underwriting at the current age, as if the policy had never existed

Evidence of insurability satisfactory to the insurer and payment of all premiums due with interest, provided the policy has not been surrendered and any automatic non-forfeiture insurance remains in force
Only the current month's premium payment, without evidence of insurability
Reinstatement is not permitted once a life insurance policy has expired for more than 30 days
B03-Q002.correctAnswer: Evidence of insurability satisfactory to the insurer and payment of all premiums due with interest, provided the policy has not been surrendered and any automatic non-forfeiture insurance remains in force
B03-Q002.explanation: For a standard life policy subject to Texas non-forfeiture rules, reinstatement is permitted within three years of default if the policy has not been surrendered, if any other insurance purchased with the value of the policy remains in force, if the insurer receives evidence of insurability satisfactory to the insurer, and if any delinquent premiums are paid with interest. This restores the original contract rather than issuing an entirely new policy.

optionExplanations.A new application with full underwriting: Rehabilitation restores the original policy rather than requiring an entirely new policy to be issued at the current age. The insurer may require evidence of current insurability, but the contract being revived is the original policy.
optionExplanations.Only the current month's premium payment: Payment of a single current premium is not enough. The insurer generally demands all premiums due with interest and satisfactory evidence of insurability before reinstating a lapsed life policy.
optionExplanations.Reinstatement is not permitted once a li: Texas life policies subject to the standard rehabilitation provision allow rehabilitation well beyond 30 days. The standard period is three years after the breach, provided other legal conditions are met.

B03-Q008.question: A small employer offers group health insurance that includes a 90-day trial period for new employees. A newly hired employee needs medical care during the first 60 days of employment. What is the employee's coverage status?
options: The employee is covered immediately upon hire because group plans cannot impose probationary periods
The employee is not yet eligible for the group plan because they have not completed the 90-day trial period
The employee is covered but must pay triple the standard premium during the probationary period
The employee is covered only for emergency services during the probationary period
B03-Q008.correctAnswer: The employee is not yet eligible for the group plan because they have not completed the 90-day trial period
B03-Q008.explanation: A probationary period (also called a waiting period or eligibility waiting period) is the length of time a new employee must wait before being eligible for group health benefits. During this period, the employee is not covered under the group plan. The employee would have to rely on other coverage (individual insurance, COBRA from a previous employer, Marketplace coverage, etc.) until the probationary period ends and group coverage begins.

optionExplanations.The employee is covered immediately upon: Group health plans may impose probationary periods for new employees, subject to applicable limits. Under the ACA, the maximum waiting period for group health plans is 90 days. The employer's 90-day period falls within this limit.
optionExplanations.The employee is covered but must pay tri: There is no provision for triple premium coverage during a trial period. The employee is simply not eligible for group benefits until completing the probationary period.
optionExplanations.The employee is covered only for emergen: The group plan does not provide partial or emergency-only coverage during the trial period. The employee is not yet a covered member of the plan.

B03-Q005.question: An applicant for a life insurance policy pays the initial premium at the time of application and receives a conditional receipt. The applicant is then determined to be insurable as requested. Under conditional receipt, when does coverage begin?
options: On the date the policy is delivered to the applicant
On the date the insurer issues the policy
On the date of application or the date of medical examination, whichever is later, provided the applicant is determined to be insurable as requested
Thirty days after submitting the application, regardless of the underwriting decision
B03-Q005.correctAnswer: On the date of application or the date of medical examination, whichever is later, provided the applicant is determined to be insurable as requested
B03-Q005.explanation: A conditional receipt states that if the applicant pays the initial premium at the time of application and is determined to be insurable as requested, coverage is effective retroactively to the date of application or the date of the medical examination, whichever is later. This protects the applicant during the underwriting period. If the applicant is not insurable as requested, the premium is returned and no coverage existed.

optionExplanations.On the date the policy is delivered to t: Under a conditional receipt, coverage does not wait until delivery of the policy. The retroactive effective date is the key advantage of conditional receipt over simply waiting for delivery.
optionExplanations.On the date the insurer issues the polic: The date of issue of the policy is not the determining date under a conditional receipt. Coverage goes back to the date of application or medical examination, not the administrative date of issuance.
optionExplanations.Thirty days after submitting the applica: Conditional receipt does not provide automatic coverage after 30 days regardless of insurability. The condition is that the applicant must be considered insurable as requested. If not, there was no coverage.

B03-Q013.question: An individual health insurance policy has been in effect for four years. The insurer finds that the insured made a material but non-fraudulent misrepresentation in the application regarding a pre-existing condition. Can the insurer use this misrepresentation to deny a claim?
options: Yes, because health insurers can deny claims based on application misrepresentations at any time
Yes, but only if the misrepresentation was fraudulent
No, because the time limit provision on certain defenses (typically two or three years) has expired, and the insurer can no longer use misrepresentation to deny a non-fraudulent claim.
No, because misrepresentation is never a basis for denying a health insurance claim.
B03-Q013.correctAnswer: No, because the time limit provision on certain defenses (typically two or three years) has expired, and the insurer can no longer use misrepresentation to deny a non-fraudulent claim.
B03-Q013.explanation: The time limit provision on certain defenses in health insurance states that after the policy has been in effect for the stated period (commonly two or three years), the insurer cannot use a material but non-fraudulent misrepresentation in the application to deny a claim or void the policy. Since this policy has been in effect for four years, that time limit has expired.

optionExplanations.Yes, because health insurers can deny cl: Insurers do not have an unlimited window to deny claims based on application misrepresentations. The time limit on certain defenses restricts this right after the policy has been in effect for the stated period.
optionExplanations.Yes, but only if the misrepresentation w: Fraud may be treated differently than a material but non-fraudulent misrepresentation. This question expresses that the misrepresentation was non-fraudulent, so the time limit provision prevents the insurer from using it after the stated period has passed.
optionExplanations.No, because misrepresentation is never a: Misrepresentation is a valid basis for denying claims during the period before the time limit on certain defenses expires. It's not that misrepresentation is never relevant; rather, the insurer's window to use it is limited.

B03-Q009.question: A life insurance policyholder includes a spendthrift clause in the policy. After the death of the insured, a creditor of the beneficiary attempts to seize the death benefits before they are paid. Under the spendthrift clause, what is the result?
options: The creditor can seize the entire death benefit because life insurance proceeds are always subject to creditor claims
Death benefit proceeds are protected from the beneficiary's creditors while they are held by the insurer, but once paid to the beneficiary, the protection generally ceases.
The creditor can seize 50% of the death benefit and the remaining 50% is protected
The spendthrift clause permanently protects the entire death benefit against all creditors even after payment to the beneficiary
B03-Q009.correctAnswer: Death benefit proceeds are protected from the beneficiary's creditors while they are held by the insurer, but once paid to the beneficiary, the protection generally ceases.
B03-Q009.explanation: A spendthrift clause protects policy proceeds against the beneficiary's creditors as long as the proceeds are retained by the insurer (for example, under a settlement option). Once the proceeds are paid to the beneficiary and become part of the beneficiary's general assets, protection under the spendthrift clause generally ceases, and the funds may become subject to creditor claims like any other personal asset.

optionExplanations.The creditor can seize the entire death: Life insurance proceeds retained by the insurer under a spendthrift provision are not subject to seizure by the beneficiary's creditors. The spendthrift clause exists specifically to provide this protection.
optionExplanations.The creditor can seize 50% of the death: There is no standard 50/50 split provision. The spendthrift clause protects the entire amount while it is retained by the insurer. The protection is complete while it is in force, not partial.
optionExplanations.The spendthrift clause permanently prote: The spendthrift clause does not provide permanent, lifetime protection against all creditors after payment. Once the income is distributed to the beneficiary and commingled with personal assets, protection under the clause generally ends.

B03-Q011.question: An insured is injured in a car accident caused by another driver. The insured's health insurer pays $30,000 in medical claims. The insured then recovers $50,000 from the at-fault driver's liability insurer. Under the subrogation provision in the health policy, what is the health insurer entitled to?
options: Recover the $30,000 you paid from the insured's third-party recovery
Collect the full $50,000 from the at-fault driver's insurance company
Nothing, because health insurers have no right to recover from agreements with third parties
Retroactively cancel the insured's health policy because a third party was responsible
B03-Q011.correctAnswer: Recover the $30,000 you paid from the insured's third-party recovery
B03-Q011.explanation: Subrogation allows the health insurer to recover the amount it paid in claims from the insured's recovery against the responsible third party. Since the health insurer paid $30,000, it is entitled to recover that amount from the insured's $50,000 settlement. This prevents the insured from receiving a double recovery for the same medical expenses.

optionExplanations.Collect the full $50,000 from the at-fau: The health insurer's right of subrogation is limited to the amount it actually paid ($30,000), not the full amount of the insured's recovery. The insured retains the remainder.
optionExplanations.Nothing, because health insurers have no: Many health insurance policies include subrogation provisions that explicitly give the insurer the right to recover claim payments from third-party recoveries. This is a standard contractual provision.
optionExplanations.Retroactively cancel the insured's healt: The existence of a responsible third party does not give the insurer grounds to retroactively cancel the policy. Subrogation allows you to recover paid claims, not cancel coverage.

B03-Q016.question: A Texas consumer purchases a Medicare Supplement policy during the consumer's Medicare Supplement open enrollment period. The consumer received treatment for diabetes 4 months before the policy effective date and has no prior creditable coverage. Assuming the insurer imposes the maximum waiting period allowed by law, when will diabetes-related claims begin to be covered?
options: Immediately on the policy effective date because a waiting period is never allowed during open enrollment
After a waiting period of up to 6 months from the policy effective date
After an exclusion period of 12 months from the policy effective date
Never, because pre-existing conditions can be permanently excluded
B03-Q016.correctAnswer: After a waiting period of up to 6 months from the policy effective date
B03-Q016.explanation: In Medicare supplement open enrollment in Texas, the company must sell the policy, but may impose a waiting period of up to six months before covering pre-existing conditions, unless prior creditable coverage eliminates or reduces that waiting period. Because the consumer received treatment within the previous six months and has no prior creditable coverage, the maximum waiting period allowed by law is up to six months.

optionExplanations.Immediately on the policy effective date: During Medicare supplement open enrollment in Texas, guaranteed issue applies, but a waiting period of up to six months may still be imposed in some cases for pre-existing conditions. Open enrollment does not automatically eliminate any waiting period.
optionExplanations.After an exclusion period of 12 months f: A 12-month pre-existing condition exclusion is not the rule for Medicare supplement open enrollment in Texas. The maximum waiting period is up to six months, not 12 months.
optionExplanations.Never, because pre-existing conditions c: Pre-existing conditions cannot be permanently excluded in this context. The issue is a temporary waiting period, not a permanent denial of coverage.

B03-Q012.question: A policyholder purchases a whole life policy and pays premiums substantially above the 7-payment test limit for the first three years. The policy is classified as a modified endowment contract (MEC). How does MEC status affect policy distributions?
options: Distributions are always received completely tax-free no matter how much was contributed
Distributions are taxed under the last-in, first-out (LIFO) method, meaning earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income, and a 10% penalty may apply if the policyholder is under age 59½.
The policy loses its death benefit and functions only as an investment account
MEC status has no effect on taxation; All life insurance is taxed identically
B03-Q012.correctAnswer: Distributions are taxed under the last-in, first-out (LIFO) method, meaning earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income, and a 10% penalty may apply if the policyholder is under age 59½.
B03-Q012.explanation: When a life insurance policy is classified as MEC (for failing the 7-payment test), distributions (including loans and withdrawals) are taxed under the LIFO method: earnings are considered to come out first and are taxed as ordinary income. Additionally, a 10% tax penalty applies to the taxable portion of the distributions if the policyholder is under age 59½. The death benefit remains income tax free for the beneficiary, but the tax treatment of living benefits changes significantly.

optionExplanations.Distributions are always received comple: Distributions from an MEC are not tax-free. LIFO treatment means that the retained earnings are taxed first as ordinary income. Only non-MEC policies enjoy first-in, first-out (FIFO) treatment, where the basis comes first.
optionExplanations.The policy loses its death benefit and f: MEC status does not eliminate the death benefit. The policy remains a life insurance contract with a death benefit. The change is in how loans and withdrawals are taxed during the life of the policyholder.
optionExplanations.MEC status has no effect on taxation; Al: MEC status has a significant effect on taxation. Non-MEC policies allow loans and withdrawals under FIFO (basis comes out first, generally tax-free to basis). MECs use LIFO, making distributions taxable and potentially subject to penalties.

B03-Q015.question: The owner of a whole life insurance policy can choose to pay premiums annually, semi-annually, quarterly, or monthly. If the policyholder switches from annual payments to monthly payments, what is the typical effect on the total annual premium cost?
options: Total annual cost decreases due to the convenience of smaller payments
The total annual cost increases because the insurer adds a service charge or frequency surcharge factor to the most frequent payment methods
The total annual cost remains exactly the same regardless of payment frequency
The insurer refunds a portion of the premium when the policyholder switches to monthly payments
B03-Q015.correctAnswer: The total annual cost increases because the insurer adds a service charge or frequency surcharge factor to the most frequent payment methods
B03-Q015.explanation: When a policyholder selects a more frequent payment mode (monthly instead of annually), the insurer typically adds a service charge or frequency surcharge factor. This means that the sum of 12 monthly payments will exceed the single annual premium. The annual mode is the least expensive way to pay because the insurer has use of the entire premium from the beginning of the year.

optionExplanations.Total annual cost decreases due to the c: More frequent payments do not reduce the cost. They increase the total annual cost due to the insurer's additional administrative expenses and the loss of investment income from not receiving the full annual premium up front.
optionExplanations.The total annual cost remains exactly th: The total annual cost does not remain the same. The frequency surcharge means the policyholder pays more overall when they choose monthly instead of annual payment. Only the amount of each payment is less.
optionExplanations.The insurer refunds a portion of the pre: The insurer does not refund a portion of the premium for switching to monthly mode. In any case, the added cost increases due to the surcharge factor.

B03-Q019.question: A point-of-service (POS) plan combines features of which two managed care models?
options: HMO and PPO
Compensation and Workers' Compensation
Medicare Advantage and Medigap
COBRA and long-term care insurance
B03-Q019.explanation: A point-of-service (POS) plan combines features of an HMO and a PPO. Like an HMO, the POS plan assigns a primary care physician and encourages the use of a network of providers. Like a PPO, it allows the member to receive out-of-network care at a higher out-of-pocket cost. The member chooses at the point of service whether to use in-network (similar to HMO) or out-of-network (similar to PPO) care.

optionExplanations.Compensation and Workers' Compensation: Indemnity insurance and Workers' Compensation are fundamentally different products and are not managed care models. A POS plan does not combine these.
optionExplanations.Medicare Advantage and Medigap: Medicare Advantage and Medigap are Medicare-related products, not the basic components of a POS plan. Although Medicare Advantage can use managed care structures, the POS concept is defined by its hybrid HMO/PPO nature.
optionExplanations.COBRA and long-term care insurance: COBRA is a continuation coverage law, and long-term care insurance is a separate product line. Neither is a managed care model that contributes to POS design.

B03-Q017.question: The owner of a life insurance policy names her husband as the primary beneficiary. Both the insured and the husband die in the same car accident, and it cannot be determined who died first. The policy contains a common disaster clause that requires the beneficiary to survive the insured by 30 days. What happens to the death benefit?
options: The income is paid to the husband's estate because he was the named primary beneficiary
The proceeds are paid as if the primary beneficiary had predeceased the insured, passing to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate.
The insurer permanently retains the death benefit
The income is divided equally between the assets of the insured and the assets of the beneficiary
B03-Q017.correctAnswer: The proceeds are paid as if the primary beneficiary had predeceased the insured, passing to the contingent beneficiary or the insured's estate.
B03-Q017.explanation: The common disaster clause (also called a survivorship clause) requires that the beneficiary survive the insured for a specific period (here, 30 days). If the beneficiary does not survive that period, the income is distributed as if the primary beneficiary had predeceased the insured. If a contingent beneficiary was named and is alive, that person receives the income. Otherwise, the proceeds go to the insured's estate.

optionExplanations.The income is paid to the husband's esta: The common disaster clause prevents this result. Since the husband did not survive the insured by 30 days, he is treated as if he had predeceased the insured. The income does not go to the husband's estate.
optionExplanations.The insurer permanently retains the deat: The insurer does not retain death benefits. Proceeds must be paid according to the policy's hierarchy of beneficiaries. The common disaster clause simply redirects the payment away from a beneficiary who did not survive the required period.
optionExplanations.The income is divided equally between th: There is no standard provision that divides proceeds between estates in a common disaster. The survivorship clause directs all income to the next beneficiary in the hierarchy.

B03-Q020.question: Insurance contracts are considered adhesion contracts because:
options: Both the insurer and the applicant negotiate each term of the contract equally
The insurer writes the contract and the applicant must accept or reject it as written, without negotiating individual terms
The contract must be physically attached to the application to be valid
The contract automatically adheres to the laws of all states in the country
B03-Q020.correctAnswer: The insurer writes the contract and the applicant must accept or reject it as written, without negotiating individual terms
B03-Q020.explanation: An adhesion contract is one prepared completely by one party (the insurer) and offered to the other party (the applicant) on an accept-it-or-leave-it basis. The applicant has no opportunity to negotiate individual provisions. Because of this unequal bargaining position, courts interpret any ambiguity in the contract language in favor of the insured (the adhering party).

optionExplanations.Both the insurer and the applicant negot: Equal negotiation describes a commercial contract between independent parties, not a contract of adhesion. Insurance contracts are not negotiated individually between the insurer and each applicant.
optionExplanations.The contract must be physically attached: The term 'accession' does not refer to a physical union. It refers to the legal concept that one party adheres to (accepts) the terms fully drafted by the other party.
optionExplanations.The contract automatically adheres to th: Accession has nothing to do with multistate applicability. Insurance contracts are governed by the law of the state where the contract is issued or delivered, not by that of all states.

B03-Q022.question: Under a standard individual health insurance policy, within how many days of a covered loss must the insured submit written proof of loss to the insurer?
options: Within 10 days of loss
Within 20 days of loss
Within 90 days of the loss, but not later than one year (except in the absence of legal capacity)
There is no time limit to submit proof of loss
B03-Q022.correctAnswer: Within 90 days of the loss, but not later than one year (except in the absence of legal capacity)
B03-Q022.explanation: The standard proof of loss provision in individual health insurance policies requires the insured to submit written proof of loss within 90 days from the date of loss. However, the claim is not barred if the evidence is presented up to one year after the deadline, unless the insured lacked legal capacity. This standard is part of the Uniform Provisions for Individual Accident and Sickness Policies.

optionExplanations.Within 10 days of loss: Ten days is the typical claim notice requirement (notification that a loss occurred), not the proof of loss deadline. Proof of loss (detailed documentation) must be submitted within 90 days.
optionExplanations.Within 20 days of loss: Twenty days is the standard period within which the insurer must provide proof of loss forms after receiving the claim notice. The insured's deadline to submit completed proof is 90 days from the loss.
optionExplanations.There is no time limit to submit proof o: Yes there is a time limit. The standard is 90 days, with a maximum extension of one year except in cases of legal incapacity. Indefinite presentation is not permitted under the standard provision.

B03-Q021.question: A member of a Texas HMO is denied a request for a specific medical procedure because it is not medically necessary. The member does not agree with the determination. Under Texas law, what is the enrollee's first step in challenging the denial?
options: File a lawsuit directly in state district court
File a complaint with the Federal Trade Commission
File an internal appeal through the HMO's grievance and appeals process
Disenroll from the HMO and immediately switch to an indemnity plan
B03-Q021.correctAnswer: File an internal appeal through the HMO's grievance and appeals process
B03-Q021.explanation: Texas law requires HMOs to maintain internal grievance and appeal procedures. When a member disagrees with a denial of coverage, the first step is to use the HMO's internal appeals process. If the internal appeal does not resolve the dispute, the member may then seek external review through an independent review organization (IRO) or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Insurance.

optionExplanations.File a lawsuit directly in state distric: Filing a lawsuit is generally not the first step. The member must first exhaust the HMO's internal appeals process. Texas law provides for internal appeals followed by independent external review prior to litigation.
optionExplanations.File a complaint with the Federal Trade: The Federal Trade Commission does not handle individual HMO medical necessity disputes. Insurance regulation in Texas falls under the Texas Department of Insurance, and the HMO's internal appeal is the initial step.
optionExplanations.Disenroll from the HMO and immediately s: Disenrollment does not resolve the coverage dispute. The member has the right to challenge the denial through the HMO's internal process and, if necessary, through external review.

B04-Q004.question: A 60-year-old person inherits $100,000 and decides to purchase a Single Premium Immediate Annuity (SPIA). When will the first payment of this annuity typically begin?
options: Within 12 months from the date of purchase
Exactly one year from the date of purchase
When the annuitant turns 65
At any time determined by the annuitant, without restriction
B04-Q004.correctAnswer: Within 12 months from the date of purchase
B04-Q004.explanation: An immediate annuity is designed to begin payments no later than one year after purchase. In practice, payments usually start much earlier, such as a month after purchase, but the defining rule is that they start within 12 months.

optionExplanations.Exactly one year from the date of purcha: The first payment does not have to start exactly one year later; the defining line is within 12 months.
optionExplanations.When the annuitant turns 65: Waiting until age 65 would make the product work as a deferred annuity, not an immediate annuity.
optionExplanations.At any time determined by the annuitant,: Immediate annuities do not allow for an open and unrestricted delay in the start of payments.

B04-Q002.question: An employer offers a group disability income policy to its employees. The employer pays 60% of the premium, and the employee pays the remaining 40% with after-tax dollars. If the employee becomes disabled and receives a monthly benefit of $5,000, what portion of this monthly benefit is subject to federal income tax?
B04-Q002.explanation: Disability income benefits are taxable in proportion to the premium paid in pre-tax dollars or by the employer. Because the employer paid 60% of the premium, 60% of the benefit is taxable. Sixty percent of $5,000 is $3,000.

optionExplanations.$0: That would be true only if the employee had paid 100% of the premium with after-tax dollars.
optionExplanations.$2,000: $2,000 is the portion attributable to the employee's premium contribution with after-tax dollars, which is generally received tax-free.
optionExplanations.$5,000: That would be true only if the employer had paid 100% of the premium.

B03-Q023.question: A 36-year-old applicant requests that her new whole life policy be backdated by four months to obtain a lower premium based on her age on that earlier date. The insurer accepts. What limitation normally applies to retroactive dating?
options: Retroactive dating is prohibited under all circumstances
Backdating is permitted, but generally limited to no more than 6 months, and the applicant must pay premiums for the backdating period.
Backdating is allowed for up to 3 years if the applicant can prove that she was in good health during the entire period.
Retroactive dating is allowed only for term life policies, not whole life.
B03-Q023.correctAnswer: Backdating is permitted, but generally limited to no more than 6 months, and the applicant must pay premiums for the backdating period.
B03-Q023.explanation: Backdating a life insurance policy to obtain a lower premium based on a younger issuance age is generally allowed, but most states (including Texas) limit backdating to no more than 6 months. The applicant must pay premiums for the entire look-back period, which means the policy is treated as if it had been issued on the previous date. This practice benefits the applicant through a lower premium based on age.

optionExplanations.Retroactive dating is prohibited under a: Retroactive dating is not prohibited. It is a recognized industry practice that benefits applicants by preserving a younger issuance age. The practice is regulated, not prohibited.
optionExplanations.Backdating is allowed for up to 3 years: A 3-year lookback window would be excessive and is not standard. The typical regulatory limit is 6 months. A longer retroactive dating would create an unreasonable gap between the policy date and the actual date of issue.
optionExplanations.Retroactive dating is allowed only for t: Retroactive dating is not limited to term policies. It can apply to any type of life insurance policy where a younger issuance age results in a lower premium, including whole life.

B04-Q007.question: An applicant completes a life insurance application, pays the initial premium and receives a conditional receipt on June 1. A required medical exam is completed on June 5. On June 10, before the insurer approves the policy, the applicant dies in an accident. During claim review, the insurer determines that the claimant met all underwriting standards as of June 5. What action will the insurer take?
options: Deny the claim and refund the premium, because the policy was never officially issued.
Pay the full death benefit, because coverage became effective on the date of the medical exam.
Pay only a portion of the death benefit, because the applicant died during the underwriting period.
Deny the claim, because conditional receipts do not cover accidental death.
B04-Q007.correctAnswer: Pay the full death benefit, because coverage became effective on the date of the medical exam.
B04-Q007.explanation: Under the standard examination approach on a conditional receipt, temporary coverage may become effective on the later of the date of application or the date of the required medical examination, provided the applicant is found to be insurable under the insurer's underwriting standards. Because the applicant is determined to be insurable as of June 5, coverage is treated as in effect prior to the June 10 death.

optionExplanations.Deny the claim and refund the premium, b: A conditional receipt exists precisely to create potential interim coverage prior to the formal issuance of the policy, subject to its conditions.
optionExplanations.Pay only a portion of the death benefit,: The death benefit is not prorated simply because the death occurred during underwriting.
optionExplanations.Deny the claim, because conditional rece: A conditional receipt is not limited to accidental or non-accidental death. If the conditions of receipt are met and the applicant is deemed insurable, full coverage may take effect prior to formal issuance of the policy.

B04-Q008.question: Under the Uniform Individual Accident and Sickness Policy Provisions Law, how many days does an insured typically have to provide a written Notice of Claim to the insurer after a covered loss occurs?
options: 15 days
20 days
60 days
90 days
B04-Q008.explanation: The standard Notice of Claim provision generally requires written notice within 20 days after a covered loss, or as soon as reasonably possible after that.

optionExplanations.15 days: 15 days is associated with the insurer's obligation to provide claim forms after receiving notice, not the insured's notice period.
optionExplanations.60 days: 60 days is associated with concepts of lawsuit/legal action, not with the initial notice of claim period.
optionExplanations.90 days: 90 days is associated with proof of loss, not notice of claim.

B04-Q010.question: A tech startup purchases a Key Person life insurance policy on its lead software developer to protect against the financial impact of that employee's premature death. In this arrangement, who typically fills the roles of policyholder, premium payer, and beneficiary?
options: The developer is the owner and payer; the startup is the beneficiary.
The startup is the owner, payer and beneficiary.
The startup is the owner and payer; The developer's family is the beneficiary.
The developer is the owner; the startup is the payer and beneficiary.
B04-Q010.correctAnswer: The startup is the owner, payer and beneficiary.
B04-Q010.explanation: In a classic key-person arrangement, the company owns the policy, pays the premiums, and is the beneficiary because the policy is intended to compensate the company for the loss of a key employee.

optionExplanations.The developer is the owner and payer; th: The employee is usually neither the owner nor the payer of premiums in a key-person arrangement.
optionExplanations.The startup is the owner and payer; The: If the family were the beneficiary, the structure would not be the usual key-person configuration.
optionExplanations.The developer is the owner; the startup: The company, not the employee, is generally the policyholder in a key-person arrangement.

B04-Q014.question: When designing an individual disability income insurance policy, how does the length of the elimination period relate to the cost of the policy premium?
options: A longer elimination period results in a higher premium.
A longer elimination period results in a lower premium.
The elimination period affects only the duration of the benefit, not the premium.
A shorter elimination period reduces the premium because the insurer pays fewer short-term claims.
B04-Q014.correctAnswer: A longer elimination period results in a lower premium.
B04-Q014.explanation: The elimination period works like a time deductible. If the insured agrees to wait longer before benefits begin, the insurer takes on less short-term risk, so the premium is lower.

optionExplanations.A longer elimination period results in a: The relationship is inverse, not direct. A longer elimination period reduces the premium.
optionExplanations.The elimination period affects only the: The elimination period is an important pricing factor; it does not only affect the duration of the benefit.
optionExplanations.A shorter elimination period reduces the: A shorter elimination period generally increases, not reduces, the premium because the insurer may have to start paying sooner.

B04-Q017.question: A policyholder can no longer pay the premiums on a whole life policy and wants a non-lapse option that maintains exactly the same face amount of death benefit, even though the coverage may eventually expire. Which option fits that objective?
options: Cash Surrender Value Option
Paid reduced life option
Extended term option
One-year term dividend option
B04-Q017.explanation: Extended term insurance uses the cash value of the policy to purchase temporary coverage at the same original face amount for as long as the cash value can sustain it.

optionExplanations.Cash Surrender Value Option: The cash surrender terminates the policy in exchange for the cash value, so no death benefit remains.
optionExplanations.Paid reduced life option: Paid reduced life keeps coverage in place permanently, but at a reduced face amount.
optionExplanations.One-year term dividend option: A one-year term dividend option is a dividend election, not the standard non-forfeiture option used when the holder stops paying premiums.

B04-Q015.question: To avoid the general 10% IRS penalty for premature distributions from a qualified retirement plan or traditional IRA, a person generally must wait until what age to withdraw funds?
options: Age 55
Age 62
Age 65
B04-Q015.explanation: The general age threshold to avoid the 10% premature distribution penalty is age 59 1/2, unless a specific exception applies.

optionExplanations.Age 55: Age 55 is relevant to a specific separation exception, not the general rule.
optionExplanations.Age 62: Age 62 is associated with Social Security, not the general penalty threshold for qualified plans.
optionExplanations.Age 65: Age 65 is a common retirement marker, but it is not the general tax penalty threshold.

B04-Q012.question: Three years after issuing a life insurance policy, an insurer discovers that the insured intentionally lied about a severe heart condition on the original application. Then the insured dies of a heart attack. How will the insurer respond to the claim under the incontestability clause?
options: Deny the claim and refund all premiums because the lie was intentional fraud.
Deny the claim but withhold the premiums because the insured committed fraud.
Pay the full death benefit because the incontestability period has expired.
Pay a reduced death benefit equal to what the premium would have purchased if the truth had been known.
B04-Q012.correctAnswer: Pay the full death benefit because the incontestability period has expired.
B04-Q012.explanation: Once the standard life insurance incontestability period has expired, the insurer generally cannot deny the claim based on misrepresentations in the application, except for nonpayment of premium. At three years, the policy is beyond the ordinary contestability period.

optionExplanations.Deny the claim and refund all premiums b: After the life policy's incontestability period expires, the insurer generally cannot deny the claim based on the misrepresentation of the application.
optionExplanations.Deny the claim but withhold the premiums: Withholding premiums while the claim is denied is inconsistent with the usual effect of the expired incontestability period.
optionExplanations.Pay a reduced death benefit equal to wha: That adjustment is associated with misrepresentation of age or sex, not the ordinary treatment of a prohibited challenge based on a misrepresentation of health after the incontestability period.

B04-Q022.question: A dentist purchases a Business Overhead Expense (BOE) disability policy to ensure that her clinic's rent and her employees' salaries are paid if she becomes disabled. How are the premiums and benefits of this BOE policy treated for tax purposes?
options: Premiums are tax deductible; Profits are received tax-free.
Premiums are not tax deductible; Profits are received tax-free.
Premiums are tax deductible; Profits are taxable as business income.
Premiums are not tax deductible; Profits are taxable as business income.
B04-Q022.correctAnswer: Premiums are tax deductible; Profits are taxable as business income.
B04-Q022.explanation: Business overhead expense premiums are generally treated as a deductible business expense. Because of that deduction, profits paid to cover general business expenses are generally taxable to the business when received.

optionExplanations.Premiums are tax deductible; Profits are: If premiums are deducted, benefits are generally not received tax-free.
optionExplanations.Premiums are not tax deductible; Profits: That answer is wrong on both sides for the usual BOE tax treatment.
The standard examination treatment for BOE is deductible premiums with taxable benefits, not non-deductible premiums.

B04-Q024.question: A person is making monthly premium payments into a deferred annuity to accumulate a retirement fund. In the context of annuities, this period of time over which funds are paid and interest grows tax deferred is known as the:
options: Annualization period
Accumulation period
Settlement period
Grace period
B04-Q024.explanation: The accumulation period is the payment/growth phase of a deferred annuity, during which premiums are paid and values ​​grow tax deferred.

optionExplanations.Annualization period: Annualization is the payment phase, not the premium construction phase.
optionExplanations.Settlement period: Settlement is used for the payment/depletion side, not the accumulation side.
optionExplanations.Grace period: Grace period refers to the late premium period in a policy, not the growth phase of an annuity.

B04-Q018.question: In a major medical insurance policy, what is the primary function of the stop-loss limit (maximum out-of-pocket provision)?
options: Limits the maximum lifetime benefit the insurer will pay.
Requires the insurer to pay 100% of covered expenses once the insured's out-of-pocket costs reach a specified amount.
Prevents the insured from filing additional claims for the remainder of the year.
Determines the initial deductible that the insured must pay before coinsurance begins.
B04-Q018.correctAnswer: Requires the insurer to pay 100% of covered expenses once the insured's out-of-pocket costs reach a specified amount.
B04-Q018.explanation: The stop-loss limit protects the insured from catastrophic out-of-pocket expenses. Once the insured's covered deductibles and coinsurance reach the established threshold, the insurer typically pays 100% of the additional covered expenses for the remainder of the period.

optionExplanations.Limits the maximum lifetime benefit the: That describes a lifetime maximum or plan payment limit, not the insured's out-of-pocket limit.
optionExplanations.Prevents the insured from filing additio: The stop-loss provision does not block future claims; improves coverage after threshold is reached.
optionExplanations.Determines the initial deductible that t: The deductible is a portion of the cost sharing, but the stop-loss limit is the overall limit of the insured's covered out-of-pocket expense obligation.

B05-Q002.question: Under the mandatory provisions of the Uniform Individual Accident and Sickness Policy Provisions Law, how many days does the insured typically have to submit a formal written “Proof of Loss” to the insurer after a covered loss occurs?
options: 15 days
20 days
60 days
90 days
B05-Q002.explanation: The standard Proof of Loss provision requires the insured to submit formal written proof to the insurer within 90 days of the loss, or as soon as reasonably possible (but not to exceed one year, unless the insured is legally incapacitated).

optionExplanations.15 days: 15 days is the amount of time the insurer has to provide claim forms to the insured after receiving a Notice of Claim.
optionExplanations.20 days: 20 days is the amount of time the insured has to provide the initial “Notice of Claim” to the insurer, not the final Proof of Loss.
optionExplanations.60 days: 60 days is the waiting period the insured must observe after submitting Proof of Loss before a lawsuit can be filed against the insurer.

B05-Q003.question: An applicant completes a life insurance application, pays the initial premium and receives a conditional receipt. The insurer requires a medical exam as part of the underwriting process. The next day, before taking the required medical exam, the applicant dies in a car accident. How will the insurer handle the claim?
options: It will pay the full death benefit, because the premium was paid and the receipt was issued.
It will pay the death benefit, but will deduct the cost of the missed medical exam from the benefits.
They will deny the claim and return the premium, because the required medical exam was not completed.
It will deny the claim, because conditional receipts never cover accidental death before the policy is issued.
B05-Q003.correctAnswer: They will deny the claim and return the premium, because the required medical exam was not completed.
