B08-Q018.question: An employee exhausts the standard 18 months of COBRA continuation coverage after termination of employment. Shortly before the end of the 18-month period, the plan notifies the qualified beneficiary that the plan offers an option to convert to an individual health plan. Under federal COBRA rules, what must the plan do about that conversion option?
options: Require the beneficiary to provide evidence of insurability before enrolling in the conversion plan.

Provide the beneficiary with the option to enroll in a conversion health plan during the 180-day period ending with the expiration of COBRA, if such a conversion option is generally available under the plan.
Automatically extend COBRA for another 18 months with the same premium.
Offer a Medigap policy regardless of the beneficiary's age or Medicare status.
B08-Q018.correctAnswer: Provide the beneficiary with the option to enroll in a conversion health plan during the 180-day period ending with the expiration of COBRA, if such a conversion option is generally available under the plan.
B08-Q018.explanation: The federal COBRA law requires that, if a health plan conversion option is generally available under the plan, the qualified beneficiary must receive that option during the 180-day period that ends when the COBRA continuation period expires.

optionExplanations.Require the beneficiary to provide evide: The COBRA conversion option rule is about making the option available; is not proposed as a new evidence of insurability requirement in the COBRA statute.
optionExplanations.Automatically extend COBRA for another 1: Standard COBRA does not automatically extend another 18 months after ordinary exhaustion unless there is a separate legal basis, such as disability or a second qualifying event.
optionExplanations.Offer a Medigap policy regardless of the: Medigap entitlements are separate entitlements related to Medicare and are not the standard remedy when COBRA runs out.

B08-Q019.question: A married woman has group health insurance through her own employer and is also covered as a dependent on her husband's group health plan. If you incur a medical expense, how will the Coordination of Benefits (COB) provision determine the order of payment?
options: The plan that has been in effect the longest is primary.
Her husband's plan is primary because he is the head of the household.
Your employer's plan is the primary payer, and your husband's plan is the secondary payer.
Expenses are split equally 50/50 between the two plans.
B08-Q019.correctAnswer: Your employer's plan is the primary payer, and your husband's plan is the secondary payer.
B08-Q019.explanation: Under standard Coordination of Benefits (COB) rules, the health plan that covers a person as an employee (the primary policyholder) always pays first. The plan that covers the person as a dependent pays second.

optionExplanations.The plan that has been in effect the lon: The amount of time a policy has been in effect does not determine the primary status between an employee plan and a dependent plan.
optionExplanations.Her husband's plan is primary because he: Head of household is an obsolete concept and does not determine insurance coordination.
optionExplanations.Expenses are split equally 50/50 between: Insurance companies coordinate to ensure that up to 100% of the claim is paid, but they do not automatically split bills 50/50; the primary plan pays first up to its limits.

B08-Q020.question: A dental insurance plan pays benefits based on the geographic area's Usual, Customary, and Reasonable (UCR) charges and requires the insured to meet an annual deductible before a coinsurance percentage is applied. What type of dental plan is this?
options: A scheduled dental plan
A comprehensive or non-scheduled dental plan
A Dental Health Maintenance Organization (DHMO)
A dental plan for basic medical expenses
B08-Q020.correctAnswer: A comprehensive or non-scheduled dental plan
B08-Q020.explanation: Comprehensive or Non-Scheduled dental plans work very similar to major health insurance. Benefits are based on usual, customary and reasonable (UCR) charges, and use deductibles and coinsurance (for example, 80/20 splits for basic procedures).

optionExplanations.A scheduled dental plan: A scheduled plan pays benefits based on a specific fixed dollar amount listed in a table for each procedure, regardless of the actual UCR cost.
optionExplanations.A Dental Health Maintenance Organization: A DHMO provides prepaid care through a network of dentists, typically using copayments instead of UCR charges, deductibles and coinsurance.
optionExplanations.A dental plan for basic medical expenses: Basic medical plans are first-dollar health coverage with low limits, not a classification for dental plans.

B08-Q021.question: In insurance contracts, statements made by the applicant in the application that are believed to be true to the best of his or her knowledge, but are not guaranteed to be absolutely true, are known as:
options: Guarantees
Representations
Concealments
Waivers
B08-Q021.explanation: Statements in an insurance application are legally considered representations. A representation is a statement believed to be true to the best of the person's knowledge and belief. An insurer can only void a contract if it is proven that a representation was a material misstatement.

optionExplanations.Guarantees: A warranty is a statement that is guaranteed to be absolutely true. Failure to comply with a warranty may automatically void a contract.
optionExplanations.Concealments: Concealment is the intentional withholding of material facts that would affect an underwriting decision.
optionExplanations.Waivers: A waiver is the voluntary relinquishment of a known legal right.

B08-Q022.question: A 66-year-old person is enrolled in Medicare Part A and Part B. He or she is also covered by a High Deductible Health Plan (HDHP) through his or her employer. Are you eligible to open and contribute to a Health Savings Account (HSA)?
options: Yes, because it is covered by an eligible HDHP.
Yes, but you can only contribute up to half the standard annual limit.
No, because people enrolled in Medicare are strictly prohibited from contributing to an HSA.
No, because people over 65 cannot work and maintain employer benefits.
B08-Q022.correctAnswer: No, because people enrolled in Medicare are strictly prohibited from contributing to an HSA.
B08-Q022.explanation: To be eligible to contribute to a Health Savings Account (HSA), an individual must be covered by a high-deductible health plan (HDHP) and must NOT be covered by other comprehensive health insurance. Enrollment in Medicare immediately disqualifies a person from making additional contributions to an HSA.

optionExplanations.Yes, because it is covered by an eligibl: Having an HDHP is required, but it is not the only rule. The presence of Medicare coverage disqualifies you.
optionExplanations.Yes, but you can only contribute up to h: There is no partial contribution rule based on being 65 or older; Enrolling in Medicare stops contributions entirely.
optionExplanations.No, because people over 65 cannot work a: People over age 65 absolutely can continue working and maintain employer benefits, but they cannot contribute to an HSA if they are enrolled in Medicare.

B08-Q023.question: An individual health insurance policy contains the optional “Misstatement of Age” provision. If the insurer discovers during a claim investigation that the insured stated a younger age on the original application, how is the insurer permitted to respond?
options: Completely voiding the policy and refunding the premiums, citing fraud.
Adjusting the claim benefits to the amount that the premium actually paid would have bought at the correct age.
Paying the full claim, as long as the two-year incontestability limit has passed.
Retroactively billing the insured for the difference in unpaid premium before paying the claim.
B08-Q023.correctAnswer: Adjusting the claim benefits to the amount that the premium actually paid would have bought at the correct age.
B08-Q023.explanation: Under the optional Health Insurance Misstatement of Age provision (which mirrors the life insurance rule), the insurer does not void the policy. Instead, it equitably adjusts the benefits payable to match what the premiums paid would have purchased if the correct age had been indicated on the application.

optionExplanations.Completely voiding the policy and refund: The policy is not voided; the benefit is simply adjusted to make the contract fair.
optionExplanations.Paying the full claim, as long as the tw: The incontestability clause (Time Limit on Certain Defenses) expressly does not protect incorrect statements of age. The insurer can adjust for age at any time.
optionExplanations.Retroactively billing the insured for th: The insurer adjusts the benefit amount outward; does not issue retroactive invoices for overdue premiums.

B09-Q002.question: A life insurance policy names the insured's 12-year-old child as the sole beneficiary. The insured dies unexpectedly and the insurer receives proof that the child's aunt personally paid the funeral expenses. Before a guardian is formally appointed, what provision allows the insurer to pay those expenses directly to the aunt instead of paying all benefits to the child?
options: Common disaster clause
Ease of payment clause
Spendthrift clause (protection against creditors)
Incontestability clause
B09-Q002.explanation: The ease of payment clause allows the insurer, at its option, to pay a portion of the benefits to a family member or other person who appears to have an equitable right because they incurred expenses, such as the insured's final medical or funeral costs. This is especially useful when the named beneficiary is a minor or not in a position to receive benefits directly.

optionExplanations.Common disaster clause: The common disaster clause addresses the order of death when the insured and beneficiary die in the same event.
optionExplanations.Spendthrift clause (protection against c: A spendthrift clause protects profits against the beneficiary's creditors; does not authorize payment to someone who paid the insured's expenses.
optionExplanations.Incontestability clause: The incontestability clause limits the insurer's ability to void a policy after it has been in force for the required period.

B08-Q025.question: An insured reinstates an individual health insurance policy that expired on October 1. On October 5, the insured is diagnosed with an illness and incurs medical expenses. On October 8, the insured broke his arm in a fall. Under the standard Reinstatement provision, how will the insurer handle these claims?
options: The insurer will cover both the illness and the broken arm because the policy was reinstated before the losses.
The insurer will deny both claims due to a mandatory 15-day trial period after reinstatement.
The insurer will cover the illness but will deny the broken arm.
The insurer will cover the broken arm, but will deny the illness claim because the illness is not covered until 10 days after recovery.
B08-Q025.correctAnswer: The insurer will cover the broken arm, but will deny the illness claim because the illness is not covered until 10 days after recovery.
B08-Q025.explanation: To protect against adverse selection, the Uniform Reinstatement provision states that once a health policy is reinstated, coverage for accidental injury begins immediately, but coverage for illness is subject to a 10-day waiting period. Therefore, the broken arm (injury) is covered, but the illness (occurred on day 5) is denied.

optionExplanations.The insurer will cover both the illness: Sickness claims are excluded for the first 10 days after reinstatement.
optionExplanations.The insurer will deny both claims due to: Accidental injuries are covered immediately upon reinstatement, not delayed by a trial period.
optionExplanations.The insurer will cover the illness but w: This is exactly the opposite of the rule; injuries are covered immediately, while illness requires a 10-day wait.

B09-Q001.question: A business owner assigns his life insurance policy to a bank as collateral for a business loan. Once the loan is paid in full, the assignment is lifted and the policyholder regains all rights. This type of transfer is known as:
options: Absolute transfer
Collateral transfer
Irrevocable transfer
Viatic transfer
B09-Q001.explanation: A collateral assignment is a temporary transfer of a portion of property rights to a creditor as security for a debt. Once the debt is paid, the assigned rights revert to the policyholder.

optionExplanations.Absolute transfer: Absolute assignment is the complete and permanent transfer of all property rights to another party.
optionExplanations.Irrevocable transfer: Irrevocable usually applies to beneficiary designations, not the standard terminology for loan repos.
optionExplanations.Viatic transfer: A viatical assignment involves selling a policy to a third party when the insured is terminally ill, which is a form of absolute assignment.

B09-Q006.question: An insured has a separate accidental death and dismemberment (AD&D) policy with a principal amount of $100,000. If the insured loses sight in one eye due to a covered accident, how much will the policy typically pay?
options: $0, because vision must be lost in both eyes to activate benefits.
$50,000, which is the capital sum.
$100,000, because any dismemberment triggers the full principal sum.
$100,000, but paid in monthly installments for one year.
B09-Q006.explanation: In an AD&D policy, the principal amount is paid for accidental death or for the loss of two major parts (for example, two limbs or the sight of both eyes). The capital sum, which is normally 50% of the principal sum, is paid for the accidental loss of a limb or sight in an eye. Therefore, the insured would receive $50,000.

optionExplanations.$0, because vision must be lost in both: Loss of sight in one eye is a covered dismemberment event that triggers the capital sum benefit.
optionExplanations.$100,000, because any dismemberment trig: The entire principal amount ($100,000) is reserved for death or double dismemberment (loss of two limbs/eyes).
optionExplanations.$100,000, but paid in monthly installmen: AD&D benefits are typically paid in a lump sum, not in installments, and the amount for a single eye would be $50,000.

B09-Q003.question: What type of life insurance policy insures two or more lives, but specifically pays the death benefit only upon the death of the last surviving insured, making it an ideal tool for financing estate taxes?
options: Joint life (first death)
Survival life (second death)
Family income policy
variable universal life
B09-Q003.explanation: Survivor life insurance (also known as second death life insurance) covers two lives, but does not pay the death benefit until the second insured dies. It is frequently used in estate planning to provide liquidity to pay estate taxes that are typically due after both spouses have died.

optionExplanations.Joint life (first death): Joint life pays the death benefit when the FIRST insured dies, not the last.
optionExplanations.Family income policy: A family income policy combines whole life with decreasing term to provide monthly income if the breadwinner dies.
optionExplanations.variable universal life: Variable universal life is a permanent policy with investment subaccounts, but typically insures only one life unless a specific endorsement is added.

B09-Q007.question: Which of the following tax-advantaged healthcare accounts is funded by the employee through pre-tax payroll deductions, but is generally subject to a strict “use it or lose it” rule at the end of the plan year?
options: Health Savings Account (HSA)
Flexible Spending Account (FSA)
Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA)
Medical Savings Account (MSA)
B09-Q007.explanation: A Flexible Spending Account (FSA) is funded by the employee with pre-tax dollars for medical expenses. However, FSAs are subject to a “use it or lose it” rule, meaning that unspent funds at the end of the year (or grace period) are typically forfeited and returned to the employer.

optionExplanations.Health Savings Account (HSA): HSA funds roll over from year to year indefinitely and belong permanently to the employee.
optionExplanations.Health Reimbursement Arrangement (HRA): HRAs are funded exclusively by the employer, not the employee, and the employer decides whether the funds are rolled over.
optionExplanations.Medical Savings Account (MSA): MSAs were the predecessors of HSAs (designed for small businesses/self-employed people) and did not have a strict use-it-or-lose-it rule.

B09-Q010.question: A beneficiary elects the interest-only settlement option under a life insurance policy. Which of the following best describes how death benefits are handled under this option?
options: The insurer pays only the interest earned on profits at set intervals, while retaining the principal until a later date.
The insurer immediately pays the entire death benefit in a lump sum and sends additional interest checks each year.
The insurer pays a guaranteed amount of principal plus interest each month until the fund is depleted.
The insurer converts the benefits into a lifetime annuity that continues only for the life of the beneficiary.
B09-Q010.correctAnswer: The insurer pays only the interest earned on profits at set intervals, while retaining the principal until a later date.
B09-Q010.explanation: Under the interest-only settlement option, the insurer retains the principal of the death benefits and pays the beneficiary only the interest earned on those funds at set intervals. The principal remains with the insurer until it is subsequently withdrawn or paid under another arrangement.

optionExplanations.The insurer immediately pays the entire: A lump sum payment terminates the settlement arrangement; there would be no principal left with the insurer to generate continuous interest-only payments.
optionExplanations.The insurer pays a guaranteed amount of: This describes a fixed amount settlement option, not just interest.
optionExplanations.The insurer converts the benefits into a: This describes a lifetime income settlement option, not just interest.

B09-Q011.question: Which statement best describes how an Exclusive Provider Organization (EPO) plan typically handles non-emergency medical care obtained outside the plan's provider network?
options: Generally does not provide benefit for out-of-network non-emergency care.
Pays reduced out-of-network benefits after meeting a higher deductible.
Allows any provider to be chosen as long as the member obtains a referral first.
Pays all non-emergency out-of-network claims at the in-network rate.
B09-Q011.correctAnswer: Generally does not provide benefit for out-of-network non-emergency care.
B09-Q011.explanation: An EPO generally requires members to use the plan's network providers for non-emergency care. Unlike a PPO or POS, an EPO typically does not offer reduced benefits for routine out-of-network services; If the care is non-emergency and out-of-network, there is usually no coverage.

optionExplanations.Pays reduced out-of-network benefits aft: Reduced out-of-network benefits are characteristic of PPO and POS plans, not a typical EPO structure.
optionExplanations.Allows any provider to be chosen as long: References are more associated with HMO type models with gatekeeper and do not create out-of-network coverage in a standard EPO.
optionExplanations.Pays all non-emergency out-of-network cl: An EPO generally does not pay for out-of-network routine care at the in-network rate.

B09-Q014.question: A wife applies for a life insurance policy on her husband's life. She will pay the premiums and retain all ownership rights. This arrangement, where the applicant/holder and the insured are two different people, is known as:
options: A viatical agreement
Third party property
A collateral transfer
Fiduciary interest
B09-Q014.explanation: Third party ownership occurs when a life insurance policy is owned by someone other than the insured (for example, a spouse holding a policy on their partner, or a company holding a policy on a key executive). The third party owner must have an insurable interest in the insured at the time of application.

optionExplanations.A viatical agreement: A viatical settlement is the sale of an existing policy by a terminally ill insured to a third party.
optionExplanations.A collateral transfer: Collateral assignment is using a policy as collateral for a loan.
optionExplanations.Fiduciary interest: Fiduciary interest refers to the financial trust responsibility of a money-handling agent, not the ownership structure of a policy.

B09-Q013.question: A widower names his three adult children as beneficiaries of his life insurance policy “per stirpes.” A son dies before the insured, leaving two children of his own. When the insured subsequently dies, how will the death benefit ordinarily be distributed under a per stirpes designation?
options: The two surviving children divide the entire death benefit equally, and the descendants of the deceased child receive nothing.
The death benefit is paid entirely to the estate of the child who died first.
Each surviving child receives one-third, and the deceased child's third passes in equal shares to that child's descendants.
All four grandchildren and children share the benefits equally per capita.
B09-Q013.correctAnswer: Each surviving child receives one-third, and the deceased child's third passes in equal shares to that child's descendants.
B09-Q013.explanation: A per stirpes designation means that each side of the family receives the share that the deceased beneficiary would have received. Here, each of the three children of the insured represents a branch. The two living children receive one-third each, and the deceased child's third passes to that child's descendants in equal shares.

optionExplanations.The two surviving children divide the en: That result would be more consistent with having no contingent treatment for the deceased beneficiary's line, not with a per stirpes designation.
optionExplanations.The death benefit is paid entirely to th: A per stirpes designation passes the portion down the deceased beneficiary's line rather than paying it by default to the deceased beneficiary's estate.
optionExplanations.All four grandchildren and children shar: Sharing equally among all descendants regardless of branch would be a per capita concept, not per stirpes.

B09-Q015.question: Under Original Medicare Part A, how many days of Skilled Nursing Facility (SNF) care are covered in full (with no patient copayment) per benefit period after a qualifying hospitalization?
options: 0 days (there is a copay from day 1)
20 days
60 days
100 days
B09-Q015.explanation: Medicare Part A covers up to 100 days of skilled nursing facility (SNF) care per benefit period. However, only the first 20 days are fully covered (100% paid for by Medicare). Days 21-100 require a substantial daily patient co-payment.

optionExplanations.0 days (there is a copay from day 1): Medicare pays 100% of the cost for the first 20 days; initially there is no co-payment.
optionExplanations.60 days: 60 days refers to the fully covered duration for inpatient hospital stays under Part A, not SNF care.
optionExplanations.100 days: 100 days is the maximum length of SNF coverage per benefit period, but only the first 20 are paid in full with no copay.

B09-Q020.question: A participating whole life policyholder selects the “Accumulate with Interest” dividend option. Which of the following describes the correct tax treatment of this option?
options: Both the dividend and the interest generated are tax-free.
Both the dividend and the interest generated are taxable as ordinary income.
The dividend is tax-free, but the interest earned is taxable as ordinary income in the year it is credited.
The interest is tax-free, but the dividend itself is taxable as a capital gain.
B09-Q020.correctAnswer: The dividend is tax-free, but the interest earned is taxable as ordinary income in the year it is credited.
B09-Q020.explanation: Dividends from a policy are considered a return of overcharged premium and are therefore generally free of income tax. However, if dividends are left with the insurer to “accumulate with interest,” the interest earned on those dividends is considered investment growth and is taxable as ordinary income in the year they are credited.

optionExplanations.Both the dividend and the interest gener: The base dividend itself is not taxable.
optionExplanations.The interest is tax-free, but the divide: Dividends are tax-free, and interest is ordinary income (not capital gains).

B09-Q016.question: A person purchases a nonqualified deferred annuity with $50,000 in after-tax savings. Years later, the account has grown to $75,000. Before the annuity start date, the owner withdraws $10,000 to pay for repairs to his or her home. How is this $10,000 withdrawal treated for tax purposes?
options: It is completely tax-free because it is considered a return of principal (FIFO).
It is fully taxable as ordinary income because withdrawals are treated as Last-In, First-Out (LIFO).
It is taxed proportionally according to the exclusion reason.
It is taxed at the lowest long-term capital gains rate.
B09-Q016.correctAnswer: It is fully taxable as ordinary income because withdrawals are treated as Last-In, First-Out (LIFO).
B09-Q016.explanation: For non-qualified annuities, partial withdrawals made before the annuitization phase (during the accumulation period) are taxed under Last-In, First-Out (LIFO). This means that the IRS considers all funds withdrawn to come from taxable interest/earnings first. Since the account has $25,000 of earnings, the entire $10,000 withdrawal is taxable as ordinary income.

optionExplanations.It is completely tax-free because it is: FIFO (principal first) taxation applies to standard life insurance withdrawals, but annuities use LIFO.
optionExplanations.It is taxed proportionally according to: The exclusion reason only applies to fixed annuitization payments (monthly income stream), not to random lump sum withdrawals during the accumulation phase.
optionExplanations.It is taxed at the lowest long-term capi: Annuity earnings are always taxed as ordinary income, never as capital gains.

B09-Q021.question: In a new individual disability income policy, the “trial period” is a single period immediately following the effective date of the policy. During this specific period, which of the following statements is true?
options: Benefits are paid for accidental injuries, but not for illness.
Benefits are paid for illness, but not for accidental injuries.
No benefits are paid for illness or accidental injuries.
The policyholder may return the policy for a full refund of premium.
B09-Q021.correctAnswer: Benefits are paid for accidental injuries, but not for illness.
B09-Q021.explanation: The trial period (typically 15 to 30 days after policy issuance) is designed to protect the insurer against adverse selection. During this time, disabilities caused by illness are not covered. However, accidental injury coverage begins immediately on the policy effective date.

optionExplanations.Benefits are paid for illness, but not f: This is backwards; Illness is excluded, accidents are covered.
optionExplanations.No benefits are paid for illness or acci: Accidents are covered immediately because they cannot be anticipated (unlike an illness that someone could sense coming).
optionExplanations.The policyholder may return the policy f: The right to return the policy for a refund is the free look period, not the trial period.

B09-Q022.question: A software company purchases a Key Person life insurance policy on its lead developer. The company is the owner, payer of premiums and beneficiary. How are premiums and the death benefit treated for tax purposes?
options: Premiums are tax deductible for the company; The death benefit is taxable.
Premiums are not tax deductible for the company; The death benefit is received tax-free.
Premiums are tax deductible for the company; The death benefit is received tax-free.
The premiums are considered taxable income for the developer; The death benefit is tax-free to the company.
B09-Q022.correctAnswer: Premiums are not tax deductible for the company; The death benefit is received tax-free.
B09-Q022.explanation: In Key Person life insurance, the company cannot deduct premium payments as a business expense. Since premiums are paid with after-tax dollars, the resulting death benefit is paid to the company completely free of income tax.

optionExplanations.Premiums are tax deductible for the comp: If the premiums were deductible, the death benefit would be taxable. The IRS does not allow both a deduction and a tax-free receipt.
optionExplanations.The premiums are considered taxable inco: The developer does not own the policy and receives no direct benefit, so the premiums are not taxable income for the developer (unlike an Executive Bonus plan).

B09-Q025.question: An insured is diagnosed with a terminal illness and has a life expectancy of less than two years. Needing funds for medical care, the insured sells their life insurance policy to a third-party company for 70% of its face value. The third party becomes the new owner and beneficiary. This transaction is called:
options: Life Settlement
Viatical agreement
Accelerated Death Benefit
1035 Exchange
B09-Q025.explanation: A viatical settlement involves a terminally ill insured (viator) selling their existing life insurance policy to a third party (viator settlement provider) for an immediate lump sum less than the death benefit. The provider assumes payment of premiums and collects the full death benefit when the insured dies.

optionExplanations.Life Settlement: A Life Settlement is similar, but involves a generally healthy insured (usually an elderly person) who simply no longer wants or needs the policy.
optionExplanations.Accelerated Death Benefit: An accelerated death benefit is an endorsement that allows the insured to access a portion of their own death benefit directly from the insurance company, without selling the policy to a third party.
optionExplanations.1035 Exchange: A 1035 exchange is a tax-free transfer of funds from one insurance/annuity contract to another, not a sale.

B10-Q003.question: A policyholder makes a tax-free exchange under Section 1035, transferring the cash value of an old life insurance policy to a new one. The old policy had an outstanding loan of $15,000, which the insurer forgives/extinguishes rather than carrying it over to the new policy. How does the IRS treat the extinguished $15,000 loan?
options: It is completely tax-free because the transaction qualifies under Section 1035.
It is treated as “boot” and is taxable as ordinary income up to the amount of any gain on the old policy.
It reduces the death benefit of the new policy, but has no immediate tax consequences.
It is taxed at the long-term capital gains rate, regardless of the cost basis of the policy.
B10-Q003.correctAnswer: It is treated as “boot” and is taxable as ordinary income up to the amount of any gain on the old policy.
B10-Q003.explanation: In a 1035 exchange, if an outstanding loan is extinguished (forgiven) rather than carried over to the new policy, the IRS treats the extinguished debt as a constructive receipt of cash. This cash equivalent is known as “boot.” The boot is taxable as ordinary income up to the amount of the gain existing in the policy delivered.

optionExplanations.It is completely tax-free because the tr: Although the primary transfer of the cash value is tax-free, the extinguished loan is considered an economic benefit received by the holder, breaking the purely tax-free nature.
optionExplanations.It reduces the death benefit of the new: It does generate immediate tax consequences because the debt was eliminated.
optionExplanations.It is taxed at the long-term capital gai: Life insurance gains are taxed as ordinary income, never as capital gains.

B10-Q001.question: A father purchases a whole life insurance policy for his young son. The policy has a level premium, but automatically increases the face amount of the death benefit, usually to five times the original amount, when the child reaches a specified age (usually 18 or 21). This specific type of policy is known as:
options: Modified Whole Life Policy
Youth Jumping Policy
Guaranteed insurability policy
Policy with return of premium
B10-Q001.explanation: A Jumping Juvenile policy (also known as a Juvenile Estate Builder) is a specialized permanent life insurance product for children. Its defining feature is that the death benefit automatically increases (typically fivefold) when the insured minor reaches the age of majority, with no premium increase or evidence of insurability required.

optionExplanations.Modified Whole Life Policy: Modified whole life has premiums that start low and increase after a few years, but the death benefit remains level.
optionExplanations.Guaranteed insurability policy: Guaranteed insurability is a rider that allows additional coverage to be purchased at future dates at standard rates, but requires payment of additional premiums for each increase.
optionExplanations.Policy with return of premium: Return of premium is a feature of term life insurance that refunds premiums if the insured survives the term; it does not multiply the death benefit.

B10-Q004.question: A university purchases a single health insurance policy specifically designed to cover all of its student athletes against injuries sustained while participating in school-sponsored sports. No individual insurance certificates are issued to students, and coverage is automatically updated as the team roster changes. This is an example of:
options: Fraternal benefits insurance
Standard group major health insurance
blanket health insurance
A Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) plan
B10-Q004.explanation: Blanket health insurance is designed for groups whose membership changes frequently, such as students, common carrier passengers, or sports teams. Because the people covered change constantly, the insurer does not underwrite individually or issue individual certificates of coverage.

optionExplanations.Fraternal benefits insurance: Fraternal benefits insurance is sold by fraternal societies to their dues-paying members, not by institutions that cover transient groups.
optionExplanations.Standard group major health insurance: Standard employer group health insurance issues individual certificates of coverage to each enrolled employee.
optionExplanations.A Health Maintenance Organization (HMO): An HMO provides comprehensive health care to its enrolled subscribers in a specific geographic area, not specialized injury coverage without transitional group certificates.

B10-Q008.question: A 66-year-old employee continues to work full time for a large corporation with 500 employees. The employee is covered by the corporation's group health plan and is also enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B. If the employee incurs a medical expense, how are benefits coordinated between the two plans?
options: Medicare is the primary payer, and the employer group plan is secondary.
The employer group plan is the primary payer, and Medicare is secondary.
The two plans split the costs exactly 50/50.
Medicare is the exclusive payer because federal law ends group coverage at age 65.
B10-Q008.correctAnswer: The employer group plan is the primary payer, and Medicare is secondary.
B10-Q008.explanation: Under Medicare Secondary Payer rules, when an active employee age 65 or older is covered by a large employer plan (20 or more employees), the employer's group plan pays first and Medicare pays second.

optionExplanations.Medicare is the primary payer, and the e: Medicare would be primary only in small employer or retired employee situations.
optionExplanations.The two plans split the costs exactly 50: Primary/secondary coordination is used, not an automatic 50/50 split.
optionExplanations.Medicare is the exclusive payer because: Federal law does not terminate employer coverage at age 65.

B10-Q007.question: A group of investors is targeting older people, persuading them to take out large life insurance policies. Investors pay all premiums and are named beneficiaries, with the intention of collecting the for-profit death benefit when the seniors die. Because investors have no real financial loss upon the death of those people, this illegal scheme is known as:
options: A viatical agreement
Stranger-Originated Life Insurance (STOLI)
A life settlement
Third-party beneficiary fraud
B10-Q007.explanation: Stranger-Originated Life Insurance (STOLI) is an arrangement in which a policy is obtained for the benefit of a party who has no insurable interest, usually an investor seeking to profit from the death benefit.

optionExplanations.A viatical agreement: A viatical settlement involves the sale of an existing policy by a terminally ill insured.
optionExplanations.A life settlement: A life settlement is the sale of an existing policy that was originally obtained for a legitimate reason.
optionExplanations.Third-party beneficiary fraud: That is not the recognized term in insurance law for this scheme.

B10-Q009.question: Under the required “Change of Beneficiary” provision for an individual accident and health insurance policy, who generally has the right to change the beneficiary when the original designation is not irrevocable?
options: Only the current beneficiary
The insured, without needing the consent of the beneficiary
The insurer, when it determines that a change is equitable
Any family member who has paid a policy premium
B10-Q009.correctAnswer: The insured, without needing the consent of the beneficiary
B10-Q009.explanation: The required Change of Beneficiary provision for an individual accident and health policy reserves to the insured the right to change the beneficiary, unless the insured has made an irrevocable designation. In the ordinary case, the consent of the beneficiary is not required for an exchange, surrender, assignment or other changes to the policy.

optionExplanations.Only the current beneficiary: A revocable beneficiary does not control the policy and cannot veto a change made by the insured.
optionExplanations.The insurer, when it determines that a c: The insurer administers the contract, but does not choose beneficiaries for the policyholder.
optionExplanations.Any family member who has paid a policy: Paying a premium does not in itself create control rights over the policy, unless the person is the insured or owner with those rights reserved.

B10-Q013.question: A 55-year-old taxpayer pays out-of-pocket the premiums for an individual tax-qualified Long-Term Care (LTC) insurance policy. Under federal tax law, how are these premium payments treated if the person itemizes their deductions?
options: They are fully deductible from the first dollar.
They are never deductible because they are considered personal expenses.
They are deductible as medical expenses, but only to the extent that the total unreimbursed medical expenses exceed 7.5% of Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).
They are deductible only if the taxpayer actually receives LTC benefits during the tax year.
B10-Q013.correctAnswer: They are deductible as medical expenses, but only to the extent that the total unreimbursed medical expenses exceed 7.5% of Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).
B10-Q013.explanation: Tax-qualified LTC premiums may be treated as medical expenses, and itemized medical expenses are deductible only to the extent they exceed 7.5% of AGI, subject to other applicable tax limits.

optionExplanations.They are fully deductible from the first: They are not deductible from the first dollar.
optionExplanations.They are never deductible because they a: Qualified LTC premiums may qualify as medical expenses under federal law.
optionExplanations.They are deductible only if the taxpayer: The deduction depends on paying qualified premiums, not receiving benefits that year.

B10-Q011.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding a Cost of Living (COL) rider attached to a life insurance policy?
options: Automatically increases the death benefit based on an inflation index without requiring the insured to prove insurability.
The premium decreases when the Consumer Price Index (CPI) falls.
Allows the insured to purchase additional coverage at specific ages, provided they undergo a new medical examination.
Waives policy premiums if the insured's living expenses exceed his or her disability income.
B10-Q011.correctAnswer: Automatically increases the death benefit based on an inflation index without requiring the insured to prove insurability.
B10-Q011.explanation: A Cost of Living rider increases the death benefit based on an inflation rate, typically without requiring evidence of insurability for those automatic increases.

optionExplanations.The premium decreases when the Consumer: The clause is designed to increase benefits with inflation, not to reduce premiums if inflation falls.
optionExplanations.Allows the insured to purchase additiona: That describes a different option to purchase clause, not a COL clause.
optionExplanations.Waives policy premiums if the insured's: That is not the function of a COL clause.

B10-Q012.question: A person purchases a specialized health insurance policy that promises to pay a single, fixed lump sum of $50,000 if the insured is diagnosed with cancer, regardless of the actual cost of medical treatment. What type of policy is this?
options: A comprehensive major medical policy
A dreaded illness/critical illness policy
A hospital indemnity policy
A short-term medical policy
B10-Q012.explanation: A dreaded illness or critical illness policy pays a fixed lump sum upon diagnosis of a covered illness, such as cancer, heart attack or stroke, without tying the payment to actual medical bills.

optionExplanations.A comprehensive major medical policy: Major medical insurance pays covered expenses instead of a fixed lump sum triggered by diagnosis.
optionExplanations.A hospital indemnity policy: Hospital indemnity generally pays a fixed daily or confinement amount, not a sickness triggered lump sum like this.
optionExplanations.A short-term medical policy: Short-term medical coverage is temporary comprehensive health coverage, not a diagnosis-triggered lump sum product.

B10-Q014.question: In a life settlement transaction, a licensed life settlement broker negotiates the sale of a policy between the policyholder and a life settlement provider. Under Texas law, to whom does the life settlement broker exclusively owe a fiduciary duty?
options: To the life settlement provider (the buyer)
To the original insurance company that issued the policy
To the policyholder (the viator)
To the main beneficiary of the policy
B10-Q014.explanation: Texas law states that a life settlement broker represents only the policyholder and owes a fiduciary duty to act upon the policyholder's instructions and in the policyholder's best interest.

optionExplanations.To the life settlement provider (the buy: The broker does not represent the provider.
optionExplanations.To the original insurance company that i: The broker does not owe a fiduciary duty to the issuing insurer in this transaction.
optionExplanations.To the main beneficiary of the policy: The broker's duty is to the current owner who is selling the policy, not to the beneficiary.

B10-Q019.question: Under original Medicare Part B (Medical Insurance), once the beneficiary has met the calendar year annual deductible, what percentage of the Medicare-approved amount is the beneficiary responsible to pay as coinsurance for covered medical services?
B10-Q019.explanation: After meeting the Part B deductible, the beneficiary typically pays 20% of the Medicare-approved amount for covered services, and Medicare pays 80%.

optionExplanations.0%: Part B is not 100% coverage after the deductible.
optionExplanations.10%: 10% is less than the patient's standard coinsurance.
optionExplanations.30%: 30% is higher than the standard Part B coinsurance.

B10-Q016.question: Five years after purchasing a universal life insurance policy that successfully passed the IRS's initial 7-payment test, the policyholder exercises his or her right to significantly increase the policy's death benefit. How does this action affect the policy's tax status under IRS rules?
options: Automatically classifies the policy as a Modified Endowment Contract (MEC).
It constitutes a “material change,” which requires the policy to undergo a new test of 7 payments from the date of the change.
It has no effect because the policy has already passed the 7-payment test at the beginning.
Converts the policy from a FIFO tax structure to a capital gains structure.
B10-Q016.correctAnswer: It constitutes a “material change,” which requires the policy to undergo a new test of 7 payments from the date of the change.
B10-Q016.explanation: A material change, such as a significant increase in the death benefit, triggers a new 7-payment test under the MEC rules; the policy is re-evaluated from the date of the change rather than automatically becoming an MEC.

optionExplanations.Automatically classifies the policy as a: The policy must be retested, but does not automatically become an MEC.
optionExplanations.It has no effect because the policy has: Passing the original test does not prevent a subsequent material change from reopening the MEC assessment.
optionExplanations.Converts the policy from a FIFO tax stru: Capital gains treatment is not the applicable rule here.

B10-Q018.question: An insured names his two adult children, Alex and Brenda, as equal primary beneficiaries “per stirpes.” Alex has two children of his own. If Alex dies before the insured, and then the insured dies a year later, how will the insurer distribute the death benefits?
options: Brenda receives 100% of the profits.
Brenda receives 50%, and Alex's two children receive 25% each.
Brenda and Alex's two children receive exactly 33.3% each.
Brenda receives 50%, and the other 50% is paid to the insured's estate.
B10-Q018.correctAnswer: Brenda receives 50%, and Alex's two children receive 25% each.
B10-Q018.explanation: Under a per stirpes designation, the branch of a deceased beneficiary receives that beneficiary's share. Therefore, Brenda retains her 50%, and Alex's share of the 50% passes equally to Alex's two children.

That result would be more like a takeover by surviving beneficiary, not per stirpes.
optionExplanations.Brenda and Alex's two children receive e: Per stirpes follows the family branch rather than dividing by head among all survivors.
optionExplanations.Brenda receives 50%, and the other 50% i: The per stirpes designation directs the deceased beneficiary's share to his descendants, not back to the insured's estate.

B10-Q020.question: Under the mandatory Legal Actions provision in an individual accident and health insurance policy, the insured cannot bring an action at law or in equity to recover under the policy before what time?
options: By the 31st day after written proof of loss is provided
By the 45th day after written proof of loss is provided
By the 61st day after written proof of loss is provided
By the 91st day after written proof of loss is provided
B10-Q020.correctAnswer: By the 61st day after written proof of loss is provided
B10-Q020.explanation: Texas Insurance Code §1201.217 requires that an individual accident and health policy provide that no legal or equitable action may be brought to recover under the policy before the 61st day after written proof of loss has been provided. The same provision also prohibits filing suit after three years from the time proof of loss was required.

optionExplanations.By the 31st day after written proof of l: 31 days is not the waiting period in the Legal Actions provision.
optionExplanations.By the 45th day after written proof of l: 45 days is not the statutory waiting period to sue under the required provision.
optionExplanations.By the 91st day after written proof of l: The required waiting period is 61 days, not 91 days.

B10-Q021.question: Which disability rider is specifically designed to be attached to a universal life insurance policy to cover internal mortality and expense charges deducted from the cash value if the insured becomes totally disabled?
options: Waiver of Premium Rider
Waiver of Monthly Deduction Rider
Disability Income Rider
Payor Benefit Rider
B10-Q021.explanation: Because universal life uses monthly internal deductions instead of a single fixed premium in the same way as traditional policies, the disability-related rider used is the Waiver of Monthly Deduction rider.

optionExplanations.Waiver of Premium Rider: Waiver of Premium is the traditional clause used for fixed premium policies.
optionExplanations.Disability Income Rider: A disability income rider pays cash benefits instead of simply protecting policy deductions.
optionExplanations.Payor Benefit Rider: A Payor Benefit rider is associated with premium protection on youth policies.

B10-Q024.question: An insured names three adult children as equal “per capita” beneficiaries. A son dies before the insured, leaving two children of his own. When the insured later dies, how are benefits distributed under the per capita designation?
options: The two children of the deceased son divide the one-third share of their father/mother
The two named surviving beneficiaries each receive half of the benefits
Benefits are divided equally between the two surviving children and two grandchildren
One-third of the benefits are paid to the insured's estate and the other two-thirds to surviving children.
B10-Q024.correctAnswer: The two named surviving beneficiaries each receive half of the benefits
B10-Q024.explanation: A per capita designation distributes per capita benefits to the surviving named beneficiaries within that class. If a named beneficiary predeceases the insured, that person's descendants do not automatically take the share. Instead, the surviving named beneficiaries divide the benefits equally, so the two surviving children each receive half.

optionExplanations.The two children of the deceased son div: That describes a per stirpes outcome, where descendants inherit the deceased beneficiary's share of the branch.
optionExplanations.Benefits are divided equally between the: Per capita does not automatically include grandchildren when the named class was the insured's children and two named children survived.
optionExplanations.One-third of the benefits are paid to th: The deceased beneficiary's share does not pass to the estate when there are still surviving named beneficiaries in the class.
